tiebreaker.q: How many sonnets did William Shakespeare write?

questions.q: What do we call the letters A, E, I, O and U?
What do we call a word that means the same, or nearly the same, as another word — such as “big” and “large”?
What does the prefix “re-” mean, as in “rewrite” or “replay”?
What do we call a word formed from the first letters of several other words, such as NASA or SCUBA?
“Notebook” and “sunflower” are each made by joining two smaller words together. What is the term for a word built that way?
What do we call two words that sound exactly alike but have different meanings — like the animal “bear” and “bare” meaning uncovered?
A letter or group of letters added to the front of a word to change its meaning — such as “un-” or “pre-” — is called what?
The ending “-ology” means “the study of.” What is the study of the Earth, its rocks and its structure called?
The word “aquarium” comes from a Latin root. What does that Latin root mean?
What do we call the study of where words come from and how their meanings have changed over time?
Which punctuation mark goes at the end of a question?
What part of speech is a word that names a person, place or thing?
What part of speech is a word that shows an action, such as “run,” “jump” or “think”?
Which punctuation mark goes at the end of a sentence that shows strong feeling or excitement?
What is the plural of the word “mouse,” when you mean the animal?
What do we call a word that takes the place of a noun — words such as “he,” “she,” “it” and “they”?
In a story, which punctuation marks are placed around a speaker's exact words?
In the sentence “The hungry dog chased the ball,” which word is the adjective describing the dog?
What part of speech describes a verb, usually telling how, when or where something happens — words such as “quickly” and “yesterday”?
Every complete sentence has two main parts. One is the subject — what is the other one called?
In E.B. White's novel “Charlotte's Web,” what kind of animal is Charlotte?
Which author wrote “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” “Matilda” and “The BFG”?
Which author wrote “The Hobbit” and “The Lord of the Rings”?
Lucy Maud Montgomery's novel “Anne of Green Gables” is set on which Canadian island?
Which Louis Sachar novel follows a boy named Stanley Yelnats, sent to a desert camp where the boys must dig a hole every day?
In Gary Paulsen's novel “Hatchet,” Brian is left alone in the northern wilderness after what kind of accident?
Which American author wrote “The Adventures of Tom Sawyer”?
Which English author wrote “Oliver Twist” and “Great Expectations”?
Which American writer wrote the 1845 poem “The Raven”?
Which ancient Greek epic poem tells the story of Odysseus and his ten-year journey home from the Trojan War?
“The snow lay over the field like a white blanket.” A comparison that uses the word “like” or “as” is called what?
“By the end of lunch, the classroom was a zoo.” A comparison that says one thing simply is another, without using “like” or “as,” is called what?
“Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” What is the term for repeating the same beginning sound in a row of words?
“Buzz,” “splash” and “crunch” are all words that imitate the sound they describe. What is the term for a word like that?
“The wind whispered through the trees and the old house groaned.” What is the term for giving human qualities to something that is not human?
“This backpack weighs a ton and I have waited here forever.” What is the term for deliberate exaggeration that is not meant to be taken literally?
“It's raining cats and dogs.” What do we call an expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words in it?
“Bittersweet” and “act naturally” each put two opposite ideas side by side. What is that figure of speech called?
“I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough.” What do we call a joke built on a word having more than one meaning?
“The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain” repeats the same vowel sound in nearby words. What is the term for that?
A haiku is a poem of three lines.
The plural of “goose” is “gooses.”
A thesaurus is a book of synonyms.
An autobiography is a person's life story written by that person.
Fiction means a written account of real events, exactly as they happened.
Every word in English contains at least one of the letters A, E, I, O or U.
William Shakespeare wrote poems as well as plays.
The word “alphabet” comes from the names of the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.
In English, an adjective such as “red” changes its ending when the noun it describes is plural.
A limerick is a poem of exactly four lines.
